column2: Early prosthetic valve IE with coagulase-negative staphylococci is S. epidermidis (biofilm on the sewing ring); surgery plus vancomycin, rifampicin, gentamicin.
Enterococcus faecalis IE follows genitourinary instrumentation in older men; treat with amoxicillin plus gentamicin or ceftriaxone.
S. bovis (gallolyticus) IE is strongly linked to colorectal neoplasia; any such bacteraemia needs colonoscopy.
Typical stable angina: CT coronary angiography is first line (NICE, ESC 2024); exercise ECG is no longer used for diagnosis.
Rest pain with inferior ST depression is NSTE-ACS; serial high-sensitivity troponin (0/1 h or 0/3 h) separates NSTEMI from unstable angina.
Swollen tender leg 10 days after pelvic surgery is high-probability DVT (Wells ≥ 2): compression ultrasound. D-dimer is raised post-op anyway.
Suspected native-valve IE: blood cultures then transthoracic echo first; TOE if TTE negative with ongoing suspicion, prosthetic valves or abscess.
Near-daily palpitations with a normal ECG: 24–48 h Holter monitoring; rarer episodes need an event or loop recorder.
PND and breathlessness on less than ordinary activity but comfort at rest is chronic LVF, NYHA class III.
Pink frothy sputum and inability to lie flat is acute pulmonary oedema: sit up, oxygen, IV furosemide, nitrates if BP allows.
Post-prandial abdominal pain with normal endoscopy in an arteriopath is chronic mesenteric ischaemia ('intestinal angina'); CT angiography.
Migratory large-joint arthritis, fever and carditis after a sore throat is acute rheumatic fever; ASO titre, penicillin, aspirin, prophylaxis.
Recurrent collapse on standing in Addison's disease is postural hypotension; check lying/standing BP and fludrocortisone dose.
Fast AF with shock is unstable: synchronised DC cardioversion (up to 3 attempts), then amiodarone if it fails.
Pleuritic pain eased sitting forward with saddle ST elevation and PR depression is pericarditis: NSAID with PPI plus colchicine.
Regular narrow tachycardia after failed vagal manoeuvres in an asthmatic: IV verapamil, as adenosine may cause bronchospasm.
Anterior STEMI without timely PCI: fibrinolysis with tenecteplase (not repeat streptokinase) plus heparin, then transfer for angiography.
Pulseless broad-complex tachycardia is pulseless VT: unsynchronised shocks with CPR; correct likely hyperkalaemia.
Collapsing pulse, early diastolic murmur and displaced apex is chronic aortic regurgitation; operate once symptoms or LV dilatation appear.
Rheumatic history, malar flush, AF and a mid-diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis; anticoagulate with warfarin.
Syncope, LVH and a harsh ejection murmur to both carotids is severe aortic stenosis; valve replacement (surgical or TAVI).
Acute LVF with a new apical pansystolic murmur to the axilla 3 days after MI is acute MR from papillary muscle rupture.
In tetralogy the loud ejection murmur comes from RV outflow (pulmonary) stenosis; the large VSD is silent.
Exertional crushing pain relieved by rest within minutes is stable angina; it also responds to GTN.
Crushing rest pain > 20 min radiating to jaw/arm with sweating is acute MI until proven otherwise: ECG within 10 min and troponin.
Sudden tearing pain through to the back in a hypertensive is aortic dissection; check arm pulses, CT aortography, no thrombolysis.
Localised anterior pain reproduced by pressure over the costal cartilages is costochondritis; NSAIDs.
Pain worse on inspiration and lying flat, eased sitting forward, is acute pericarditis.
ACE inhibitors (captopril) improve HFrEF survival but cause dry cough in ~10%; switch to an ARB.
In bilateral renal artery stenosis GFR depends on angiotensin II, so ACE inhibitors can cause AKI.
Dihydropyridine CCBs (nifedipine) cause headache, flushing, reflex tachycardia and ankle oedema.
Aspirin 300 mg chewed is given as soon as ACS is suspected; a P2Y12 inhibitor is added.
Non-selective propranolol causes bronchospasm in asthma and worsens peripheral vascular disease.
An apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.
Janeway lesions and splinter haemorrhages are vascular signs of infective endocarditis.
Erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules are major Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever.
Slow-rising carotid pulse with an ejection murmur at the right upper sternal edge is aortic stenosis.
A left parasternal heave and loud P2 are signs of pulmonary hypertension; confirm with right heart catheter (mPAP > 20 mmHg).
Pansystolic murmur at the lower sternal edge with giant v waves and a pulsatile liver is TR (schistosomal pulmonary hypertension in Egypt).
AF with an apex in the mid-axillary line and a loud pansystolic murmur is chronic severe MR.
Down syndrome is associated with AV septal and ventricular septal defects; a pansystolic murmur fits a VSD.
Collapsing pulse with an early diastolic murmur loudest sitting forward is aortic regurgitation.
Graham Steell murmur: early diastolic pulmonary regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension (e.g. severe MS), louder on inspiration.
Persistent velcro crackles with clubbing in a now volume-depleted patient is pulmonary fibrosis misdiagnosed as oedema; HRCT, reduce diuretic.
Waking at night gasping and rushing to the window is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fairly specific for LV failure.
Needing several pillows to breathe at night is orthopnoea; pillow count tracks severity.
A dry cough weeks after starting an ACE inhibitor is from bradykinin; switch to an ARB after excluding pulmonary oedema.
Chronic congestion in right heart failure gives a 'nutmeg' liver and tender hepatomegaly.
ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3 is a posterior MI (mirror image); V7–V9 show elevation.
Widespread saddle ST elevation (except aVR) with PR depression is pericarditis.
ST elevation in II, III and aVF is inferior MI (RCA); check V4R and watch for AV block.
P waves unrelated to a slow broad escape rhythm (45/min) is third-degree heart block: pace.
Sawtooth flutter waves with a regular rate of 150/min is atrial flutter with 2:1 block.
Fever after dental work with a known stenotic aortic valve is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise.
Exertional dyspnoea, angina and presyncope with a loud systolic murmur at 49 is symptomatic AS (likely bicuspid): valve replacement.
Pleuritic pain with saddle ST changes on day 2 after MI is early fibrinous pericarditis; Dressler syndrome comes weeks later.
Heavy alcohol use with heart failure, functional MR and a globular heart is alcoholic DCM; abstinence may restore function.
Ankle oedema and severe limitation in COPD is cor pulmonale; LTOT and diuretics.
Pleuritic pain on the pill with tachycardia, new RBBB and raised D-dimer but normal CXR is PE; CTPA and anticoagulate meanwhile.
Meal- and posture-related burning pain relieved by antacids on an NSAID is GORD; the sagging ST depression is digoxin effect. Stop NSAID, start PPI.
